questions.stem: The First Five Year Plan (1951–56) was based on the Harrod-Domar model and gave highest priority to:

options.text: Heavy industries and machine production
Agriculture, irrigation, and rehabilitation of partition-displaced persons
Export-led industrialisation and foreign exchange generation
Rural electrification and public sector expansion

questions.explanation: The First Five Year Plan (1951–56) used the Harrod-Domar model of economic growth. It prioritised agriculture, irrigation, and power generation, along with rehabilitation of partition refugees. Major projects: Bhakra Nangal Dam (Punjab), Damodar Valley Corporation. The Plan's target growth was 2.1%; actual growth was 3.6%, making it the first plan to exceed its target. Heavy industry became the focus only from the Second Plan.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Second Five Year Plan (1956–61) was based on the Mahalanobis model, which emphasised:

options.text: Agriculture and food self-sufficiency through the Green Revolution
Rapid development of heavy and basic industries in the public sector
Small-scale industries and cottage industries to generate rural employment
Foreign investment and export diversification to boost foreign exchange

questions.explanation: The Second Five Year Plan (1956–61) was designed by Professor P.C. Mahalanobis (ISI Kolkata) and emphasised rapid development of heavy industry in the public sector to build a self-reliant industrial base. Three major steel plants were established: Bhilai (Soviet assistance), Durgapur (British), and Rourkela (West German). The Industrial Policy Resolution 1956 followed this socialist pattern, reserving heavy industries for the public sector.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Third Five Year Plan (1961–66) failed to meet its growth target mainly because of:

options.text: Drought across all states of India for three consecutive years
Failure of the Green Revolution to produce surplus food grain
The Sino-Indian War (1962) and the Indo-Pakistani War (1965), which diverted resources and caused economic disruption
A major banking crisis caused by nationalisation of private banks

questions.explanation: The Third Five Year Plan (1961–66) was severely disrupted by two wars: the Sino-Indian War (1962) and the Indo-Pakistani War (1965). Defence spending surged, resources were diverted from development, and external aid was reduced. The plan targeted 5.6% growth but achieved only 2.8%. It was followed by a 'Plan Holiday' of three annual plans (1966–69) instead of launching a Fourth Five Year Plan, as economic conditions were too unstable.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The phrase 'Garibi Hatao' (Remove Poverty) was the political slogan of the Fourth Five Year Plan period and was associated with:

options.text: Jawaharlal Nehru's 1950 election campaign
Rajiv Gandhi's 1984 election landslide after Indira Gandhi's assassination
Manmohan Singh's economic reforms package of 1991
Indira Gandhi's 1971 general election campaign and the Fourth Five Year Plan (1969–74)

questions.explanation: 'Garibi Hatao' was Indira Gandhi's iconic 1971 election slogan that helped her win a massive majority. The Fourth Five Year Plan (1969–74) coincided with major policy moves: nationalisation of 14 major banks (July 1969), Green Revolution consolidation (Punjab, Haryana wheat), abolition of Privy Purses of former princes, and targeted poverty alleviation programmes. The Plan also saw the first nuclear test (Pokhran-I, 1974, just after the plan ended).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Fifth Five Year Plan (1974–79) was terminated prematurely (before its scheduled 1979 end date) by:

options.text: The Supreme Court's ruling that Five Year Plans were unconstitutional
The Janata Party government, which came to power in 1977 after the Emergency and chose to launch its own Sixth Plan
India's Finance Minister citing non-availability of foreign funds for the plan
A natural disaster (1977 Andhra Pradesh cyclone) that forced reallocation of plan funds

questions.explanation: The Fifth Five Year Plan (1974–79) introduced the 20-Point Economic Programme and the Minimum Needs Programme. However, it was cut short by one year when the Janata Party government under Morarji Desai came to power after the 1977 general elections (following the Emergency period 1975–77). The Janata government launched a new Sixth Plan (1978–83), though this was in turn superseded when Indira Gandhi returned to power in 1980 and launched yet another Sixth Plan (1980–85).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Seventh Five Year Plan (1985–90) had the tagline 'Food, Work, and Productivity'. Its major employment scheme for rural areas was:

options.text: Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS)
Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana
Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY)
Integrated Rural Development Programme (IRDP)

questions.explanation: The Seventh Five Year Plan (1985–90) under Rajiv Gandhi focused on 'Food, Work, and Productivity'. The Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) was its flagship rural employment scheme, providing wage employment to unemployed and underemployed people in rural areas through public works creation. IRDP was part of the Sixth Plan; MGNREGS came only in 2005; PM Gram Sadak Yojana in 2000. The Seventh Plan period also saw India's IT revolution begin and the telecom expansion under Sam Pitroda.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Twelfth Five Year Plan (2012–17) was India's last Five Year Plan because:

options.text: The Supreme Court declared Five Year Planning unconstitutional in 2012
The 99th Constitutional Amendment abolished the Planning Commission
WTO rules required India to end state-directed economic planning
The NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission from January 2015, shifting from centralised Five Year Plans to a more flexible framework

questions.explanation: The Twelfth Five Year Plan (2012–17) was the last, with the tagline 'Faster, Sustainable, and More Inclusive Growth'. The Planning Commission was dissolved on 31 December 2014, and NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) was established on 1 January 2015 by the Narendra Modi government. NITI Aayog functions as a policy think-tank and advisory body rather than a fund-allocating planning authority, signalling the end of Soviet-style centralised five-year planning.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Planning Commission of India was established in March 1950. The Prime Minister is its ex-officio Chairman. The first Deputy Chairman — the working head of the Commission — was:

options.text: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
Dr. Manmohan Singh (1985–87)
P.C. Mahalanobis (as Statistical Adviser, not Deputy Chairman)
Gulzarilal Nanda, who served from 1950 to 1952 and later twice became interim Prime Minister

questions.explanation: Gulzarilal Nanda was the first Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission (1950–1952). He was a veteran freedom fighter and labour leader who played a significant role in early planning. He later served as India's Acting Prime Minister twice: after Jawaharlal Nehru's death (May 1964, briefly) and after Lal Bahadur Shastri's death (January 1966, briefly), before Indira Gandhi was elected. Dr. Manmohan Singh was Deputy Chairman in 1985–87 under Rajiv Gandhi.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The 'Plan Holiday' of 1966–69 (three annual plans instead of a Fourth Five Year Plan) was caused by all of the following EXCEPT:

options.text: Severe droughts in 1965 and 1966 affecting food production
War-induced economic disruption from the Indo-Pakistani War (1965)
Devaluation of the Indian rupee by 36.5% in June 1966 creating economic instability
A constitutional crisis caused by the Supreme Court striking down the Planning Commission's authority

questions.explanation: The 1966–69 Plan Holiday was caused by three simultaneous crises: (1) severe droughts (1965–66) requiring large-scale food imports; (2) the Indo-Pakistani War (1965) diverting resources; (3) India's devaluation of the rupee in June 1966 (by 36.5%) which caused economic disruption and reduced foreign aid. There was NO constitutional crisis or Supreme Court challenge to the Planning Commission during this period — that option is fabricated.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Eighth Five Year Plan (1992–97) coincided with the LPG economic reforms of 1991. It was India's first plan to formally acknowledge and incorporate which shift?

options.text: Replacing the GDP growth target with a human development index (HDI) target
Prioritising defence spending over social sector expenditure
Reverting to agricultural planning after the failure of industrial planning
A market-oriented approach with reduced state monopoly, trade liberalisation, and greater private sector participation

questions.explanation: The Eighth Five Year Plan (1992–97) under P.V. Narasimha Rao government formally incorporated the liberalisation, privatisation, and globalisation (LPG) framework that Manmohan Singh launched in 1991. It moved away from the earlier command-economy approach: industrial licensing was dismantled, import quotas were reduced, public sector monopoly was curtailed, and the private sector was encouraged. The plan targeted 5.6% growth and achieved 6.8% — the best performance to that point.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Eleventh Five Year Plan (2007–12) had the theme 'Faster and More Inclusive Growth'. Its GDP growth target was 9%, and actual average growth was approximately:

options.text: Around 8% — broadly close to target, the best performance of any plan up to that point
Around 5% — well below target due to the global financial crisis (2008) and poor monsoons
Around 10.5% — exceeded the target every year without exception
Around 3% — a complete failure with two years of negative growth

questions.explanation: The Eleventh Five Year Plan (2007–12) targeted 9% GDP growth. Actual performance averaged about 7.9–8% over the five years. While the global financial crisis of 2008–09 briefly slowed growth (India's GDP still grew ~6.7% in 2008–09, not declining), strong growth in other years compensated. This made the 11th Plan one of India's better-performing plans. The 'inclusive growth' emphasis introduced specific targets for education, health, and poverty reduction alongside GDP.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: NITI Aayog, which replaced the Planning Commission in 2015, differs from the Planning Commission primarily in that:

options.text: NITI Aayog can allocate funds directly to states, while the Planning Commission could only advise
NITI Aayog functions as a policy think-tank and advisory body; unlike the Planning Commission it does not have the authority to allocate plan funds to ministries or states
NITI Aayog is chaired by the Finance Minister rather than the Prime Minister
NITI Aayog has constitutional status while the Planning Commission did not

questions.explanation: The key structural difference: the Planning Commission allocated plan funds (grants and loans to states and central ministries), giving it enormous power over state governments. NITI Aayog does NOT allocate funds — this power was transferred to the Finance Ministry. NITI Aayog serves as a policy research, innovation, and advisory body. It is chaired by the Prime Minister (same as the Planning Commission). It has no constitutional status (neither did the Planning Commission — both were executive creations).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Mahalanobis model (used in the Second Five Year Plan) recommended prioritising heavy industry because of the argument that:

options.text: Agriculture had already reached full potential and further investment would yield zero returns
Foreign aid would be available exclusively for heavy industry projects
India needed to imitate China's Cultural Revolution industrial model

Only heavy industries (capital goods) could produce the machines needed to produce consumer goods and agricultural equipment, breaking the dependency on foreign capital goods imports and enabling self-sustained growth

questions.explanation: The Mahalanobis strategy argued for a 'two-sector' approach: invest heavily in capital goods industries (machine tools, steel, heavy chemicals) because they produce the very machines needed to manufacture consumer goods and agricultural inputs. Once this capital goods base was established, it would be self-perpetuating and reduce dependence on imported machinery. Critics (like B.R. Shenoy) argued this neglected agriculture and consumer goods, causing shortages. The approach mirrored the Soviet model of industrialisation.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Sixth Five Year Plan (1980–85) introduced the Integrated Rural Development Programme (IRDP) and the National Rural Employment Programme (NREP). These were significant because:

options.text: They were the first time industry was included in five-year plans
They were the first time private companies were allowed to bid for infrastructure contracts
They represented India's first comprehensive anti-poverty programmes specifically targeting rural poor households with asset creation, wage employment, and skill development
They were designed exclusively to benefit urban slum dwellers rather than rural populations

questions.explanation: The Sixth Plan (1980–85, Congress government under Indira Gandhi) marked a shift toward explicitly targeted anti-poverty interventions. IRDP provided subsidised loans and assets (cattle, tools) to Below Poverty Line (BPL) rural families; NREP provided wage employment through public works in lean agricultural seasons. Antyodaya (upliftment of the poorest of poor) was another key programme. These became templates for subsequent poverty alleviation initiatives including MGNREGS (2005).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Tenth Five Year Plan (2002–07) set a target of doubling per capita income in ten years and had an ambitious growth target of 8%. Which single significant social target was set for the first time?

options.text: Universal adult suffrage for elections held during the plan period
Achieving a 50% reduction in gender gap in literacy and wage rates
Providing free higher education to all SC/ST students by 2007
Connecting all villages to motorable roads by 2007 under Bharat Nirman

questions.explanation: The Tenth Five Year Plan (2002–07) included Bharat Nirman — a rural infrastructure programme covering roads, electrification, water supply, housing, and telephone connectivity in villages. The plan aimed to connect all villages with a population of ≥1,000 (500 in hilly/tribal areas) to motorable roads. The overall Tenth Plan achieved 7.6% average growth (target 8%), driven by IT services and manufacturing. The plan also contained the first explicit literacy gender gap reduction targets.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Ninth Five Year Plan (1997–2002) was launched under which government and carried which primary theme?

options.text: Atal Bihari Vajpayee government; theme: 'Infrastructure for Growth'
H.D. Deve Gowda / I.K. Gujral / A.B. Vajpayee governments; theme: 'Growth with Social Justice and Equity'
P.V. Narasimha Rao government; theme: 'Liberalisation and Globalisation'
Manmohan Singh government; theme: 'Inclusive and Sustainable Development'

questions.explanation: The Ninth Five Year Plan (1997–2002) was launched under H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front government (1997) and continued through I.K. Gujral's and then Atal Bihari Vajpayee's governments. Its theme was 'Growth with Social Justice and Equity'. It ran during significant economic milestones including the East Asian financial crisis (1997–98) which slowed India slightly, and the Pokhran-II nuclear tests (1998). Average growth during the plan was approximately 5.5%, below the 6.5% target.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which scheme, launched during the Fifth Five Year Plan (1974–79) period and associated with Indira Gandhi's 20-Point Economic Programme, combined land reform with direct poverty alleviation?

options.text: Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi (PM-KISAN)
National Food for Work Programme
Antyodaya (Upliftment of the poorest of the poor) and Minimum Needs Programme (MNP)
Jawahar Rozgar Yojana

questions.explanation: The Fifth Five Year Plan introduced the Minimum Needs Programme (MNP), which guaranteed every citizen access to minimum quantities of essential goods and services (food, shelter, water, health). Antyodaya targeted specifically the poorest rural households for priority access to ration cards and subsidised goods. The 20-Point Economic Programme (1975, during Emergency) included land reform, bonded labour abolition, expansion of cooperative credit, and adult literacy. Jawahar Rozgar Yojana was a Seventh Plan initiative.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Across India's Five Year Plans, which plan period recorded the LOWEST average annual GDP growth rate due to war, drought, and the 1966 currency devaluation?

options.text: First Five Year Plan (1951–56): ~3.6%
Third Five Year Plan (1961–66): ~2.8%, the lowest of any plan
Sixth Five Year Plan (1980–85): ~5.5%
Second Five Year Plan (1956–61): ~4.3%

questions.explanation: The Third Five Year Plan (1961–66) recorded India's worst plan-period performance at approximately 2.8% average growth (target was 5.6%). The three simultaneous shocks — Sino-Indian War (1962), Indo-Pakistani War (1965), and severe droughts (1965–66) — devastated the economy. The rupee was subsequently devalued by 36.5% in June 1966. This failure led directly to the Plan Holiday (1966–69). The First Plan actually over-achieved its target (3.6% vs 2.1% target).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Twelfth Five Year Plan (2012–17) had a growth target of 8%. A critic argues that the actual growth fell short because of persistent high inflation, fiscal constraints, and a slowdown in investment. The plan's theme 'Faster, Sustainable, and More Inclusive Growth' acknowledged which concern NOT prominently featured in earlier plans?

options.text: The need for English-medium education in all government schools
The importance of space technology for economic development
The need for climate change resilience and environmental sustainability as explicit plan objectives
Elimination of all state governments' separate budgetary planning to create a unified national plan

questions.explanation: The Twelfth Five Year Plan was the first to explicitly incorporate climate change adaptation and mitigation, environmental sustainability, and green growth as major planning objectives — not just as add-ons but as cross-cutting themes integrated into every sector. Earlier plans focused on economic growth with environmental concerns at the margins. The 12th Plan also emphasised quality (not just quantity) of growth: health outcomes, education quality, and regional equity alongside the GDP target.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The famous 'Gadgil Formula' for resource allocation to states (named after D.R. Gadgil, Deputy Chairman of Planning Commission 1967–71) was significant because it:

options.text: Determined the share of states in central taxes based on their industrial output
Replaced the Finance Commission's role in tax devolution
Set the exchange rate between Indian state currencies

Established criteria-based formula (population, per capita income, tax effort, special problems) for distributing plan assistance to states, replacing arbitrary negotiations between states and the Planning Commission

questions.explanation: The Gadgil Formula (introduced in 1969 for the Fourth Five Year Plan) created a systematic, criteria-based mechanism for distributing central plan assistance to states. The factors included: population (60% weight), per capita income — special weighting for backward states (10%), tax effort (10%), ongoing plan projects (10%), and special problems (10%). It replaced the previous system of bilateral bargaining between states and the Planning Commission, which often favoured politically powerful states.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: A student argues: 'The Planning Commission had constitutional status, which is why its abolition required a constitutional amendment.' This statement is:

options.text: Correct — the Planning Commission was established under Article 370 of the Constitution
Correct — the Constitution's Directive Principles mandate the existence of a planning body

Incorrect — the Planning Commission was established by an executive order of the Cabinet (1950) and had no constitutional status; it could be and was abolished simply by a government resolution without any constitutional amendment
Correct — the Planning Commission was established by an act of Parliament (Planning Commission Act, 1951)

questions.explanation: The Planning Commission was established by a Cabinet Resolution on 15 March 1950 — purely an executive act. It had NO constitutional basis. It was not created by legislation. NITI Aayog similarly was created by executive order (Cabinet Resolution, 1 January 2015) and replaced it without any parliamentary legislation or constitutional amendment. This contrasts with the Finance Commission, which IS a constitutional body under Article 280. The Constitution's Directive Principles (Article 39) call for equitable distribution of resources but do not specify a Planning Commission.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: An examiner asks: 'During which Five Year Plan did India achieve the historically significant Green Revolution, the first nuclear test, and bank nationalisation?' The answer is:

options.text: The events span two plans: Green Revolution consolidated in the Third (1961–66) and Fourth (1969–74); bank nationalisation in the Fourth (1969); Pokhran-I nuclear test in 1974 — technically just after the Fourth Plan ended
All three occurred in the Second Five Year Plan (1956–61)
All three occurred in the First Five Year Plan (1951–56)
All three occurred in the Fifth Five Year Plan (1974–79)

questions.explanation: Timeline: Green Revolution (HYV seeds in wheat) began in Punjab/Haryana in 1966–68 — during the Plan Holiday between the Third and Fourth plans — and was consolidated in the Fourth Plan (1969–74). Bank nationalisation (14 banks) occurred in July 1969, early in the Fourth Plan. India's first nuclear test (Pokhran-I, Operation Smiling Buddha) was on 18 May 1974 — technically just after the Fourth Plan ended (the Fourth Plan ran 1969–74) and at the very start of the Fifth Plan period. So they span the Third Plan Holiday and Fourth/early Fifth plan period.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Harrod-Domar growth model, used in India's First Five Year Plan, links growth rate to which key variables?

options.text: Population growth rate and birth/death ratios only
The savings rate and the capital-output ratio: Growth = Savings Rate / Capital-Output Ratio
The level of exports and the trade balance surplus
Total government expenditure divided by the number of working-age citizens

questions.explanation: The Harrod-Domar model (Roy Harrod 1939, Evsey Domar 1946) states: Growth Rate (g) = Savings Rate (s) / Capital-Output Ratio (v). To grow faster, a country must either save/invest more (higher s) or use capital more efficiently (lower v). This model was appealing to early planners because it gave a direct policy lever: increase the savings/investment rate through public sector investment. India's planners used it to calculate how much investment was required to achieve target growth rates. Its limitations (it assumed a fixed capital-output ratio) led to more sophisticated models.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Critics of India's Five Year Planning model have argued that the system created a 'Licence-Permit-Quota Raj'. Which of the following was NOT a feature of this system?

options.text: Companies had to obtain a government licence before setting up or expanding any factory under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951
Import licences were required for virtually every category of imported good, creating severe shortages and rent-seeking
The government set production quotas for private companies, deciding how much each firm could produce
State governments were prohibited from setting up any industries; all industrial licensing was exclusively reserved for the central government

questions.explanation: Option D is NOT a feature of the Licence Raj. State governments could and did set up industries — there was an extensive framework of state-level public sector units (e.g., state electricity boards, state transport corporations). The actual features of the Licence Raj were: (A) industrial licensing under IDRA 1951 — companies needed central government approval to set up, expand, or diversify production; (B) import licensing — severe controls on imports; (C) production quotas and price controls in many sectors. The system was largely dismantled after the 1991 reforms.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: NITI Aayog's 'Aspirational Districts Programme' (launched 2018) differs from Five Year Plan approaches to backward areas in which fundamental respect?

options.text: Five Year Plans focused on all districts equally; NITI Aayog focuses exclusively on the five wealthiest districts

Five Year Plans measured success by GDP growth alone; the Aspirational Districts Programme uses a composite index of health, education, financial inclusion, agriculture, and infrastructure with monthly data updates and inter-district competition
The Aspirational Districts Programme is managed exclusively by foreign NGOs under NITI Aayog supervision
Five Year Plans had no mechanism for backward area development; this is an entirely new concept with NITI Aayog

questions.explanation: The Aspirational Districts Programme identifies 112 most backward districts and uses a real-time, multi-dimensional ranking across five domains: health and nutrition, education, financial inclusion and skill development, agriculture and water resources, and basic infrastructure. Monthly champion of change rankings create competitive federalism among districts. This contrasts with Five Year Plans which used aggregate national GDP targets and backward area funds (like DRDA programmes) without real-time competitive monitoring or multi-dimensional measurement. Five Year Plans DID address backward areas (DRDA, EAS), so D is wrong.
questions.subject: Economics
